question.note: Asks whether the 'convicted criminal' labeling in the advertisement spills over onto perceptions of people with records (Q1); phrased generally ('political advertisements'), which is acceptable for a question.
Whether the stigmatizing ad affects Democrats' feelings of being represented by their party (p.3 framing).

flags.text: Says 'political advertisements using stigmatizing labels for high-profile figures' reduce perceptions. The paper tested one advertisement (Trump's mugshot labeled 'CONVICTED CRIMINAL') and says replication in other contexts is unclear (p.17).

central_claim.note: Gives the ad's harm to perceptions and the counter-narrative's mitigation; omits that the ad improved feelings of representation.

evidence.note: E2: total N and three arms. E1 partial: survey experiment with U.S. Democrats (Prolific is in entry 3). E3 partial: ad by its 'convicted criminal' label, no mugshot.
Accurate (perspective-getting counter-narrative meant to foster empathy, p.3-4); adds nothing beyond E3, which entry 6 gives.
Lists the outcome families but omits the ad-support index and the index details; 'value of representation' is a single item, not an index (minor, not flagged).
Prolific and the U.S. Democrat sample; 'survey experiment' is in entries 0 and 5. Together they give E1 (pre-registration and dates treated as detail, as in the calibration).
Without the with/without covariates detail, as in the calibration.
Counter-narrative half of E3: excerpt from a news article about a formerly incarcerated legislator (Jovan Jackson is named in the paper, p.4); redemption theme is in p.5.
A finding (counter-narrative offset the ad's effect on perceptions) placed in the evidence slot.

key_findings.note: Keeps 'before the advertisement'; the quote gives the >0.8 SD comparison with the ad alone. Magnitude is detail.

flags.text: Says the counter-narrative decreased support for 'the use of stigmatizing political advertisements'. The outcome was support for this one Trump advertisement, relative to the ad alone (p.11).

Generalizes to 'political advertisements labeling an individual as a "convicted criminal"'; the paper tested one advertisement (Trump's mugshot with the label) and says replication in other contexts is unclear (p.17).

key_findings.note: 'Associated with' is weaker than the paper's causal wording; not flagged.

flags.text: 'Exposure to a counter-narrative significantly increased the perceived value of diversity' drops that the counter-narrative came before the ad and is compared with the ad alone; there was no counter-narrative-only arm (p.10, p.16). The quote keeps the comparison.

key_findings.note: H1C (0.79 SD, p.11) is accurate but not a gold answer (same call as the calibration).

flags.text: 'Exposure to a counter-narrative significantly decreased perceived quality of Democratic representation' drops 'relative to the Trump advertisement alone'; there was no counter-narrative-only arm. The quote keeps the comparison.

key_findings.note: Public-service motives increase (correct direction), without the representation-quality increase. The quote (p.11, in the paper) speaks to the unhypothesized value and quality effects rather than motives.

scope_and_limits.note: Social desirability / Hawthorne concern is part of L4; omits that the manipulation check eases but does not rule it out. 'Single time-point survey design' is given without its consequence, so no L5 credit.
Durability ('longer periods') is part of L5; 'different electoral contexts' is vaguer than L6 (fielded after the election) and earns nothing.
States the missing counter-narrative-only arm without its consequence; entry 6 gives the consequence.
Gap to behavior/decision-making; durability is in entry 1; repeated exposure is never mentioned, so L5 is not joined (as in the calibration).
Missing arm, budget reason and the consequence (cannot isolate the counter-narrative's effect).
Repeats the social desirability concern of entry 0; no manipulation-check qualification, so L4 is not joined.

theoretical_positioning.note: Social categorization theory with homogenization and spillover; no stance stated, so no T4 (as in the calibration).
Perspective-getting literature as the grounding of the counter-narrative intervention (p.3).

interlocutor_claim.note: Garbles I4: the cited study [33] found anger-inducing ads bolster support among the producing party's members; the entry gives this as a rationale the party might have had, which is how the paper uses it (p.3), but not the study's finding itself.
Garbled wording ('negative campaigning does not empirically support election success'), but the substance is the meta-analytic claim [7] the paper builds on.

flags.text: Says the author disputes that negative campaign ads are ineffective. The paper builds on the meta-analytic evidence that negative ads do not aid election success (p.2), and it qualifies the emotional-mobilization literature [30-32] ('this is not necessarily concrete', p.3) rather than endorsing it against I2.
